q: When two bodies at different temperatures are placed in contact, thermal energy flows on its own from the body with the:
o: Greater internal energy to the one with less internal energy
Larger mass to the one with smaller mass
Higher temperature to the one at lower temperature
Higher specific heat to the one with lower specific heat
x: Heat flows spontaneously from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature. A body with more internal energy (for example a large cold object) can still be at the lower temperature.

q: A hot body and a cold body are placed in contact inside a perfectly insulated box until they reach a common temperature. Which statement is correct?
o: Both bodies change temperature by the same amount
The heat lost by the hot body equals the heat gained by the cold body
The cold body gains more heat than the hot body loses
The final temperature is always the average of the two starting temperatures
x: With no heat lost to the surroundings, energy is conserved: heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body. The temperature changes are equal only if the two bodies have equal heat capacities.

q: According to the kinetic theory, the temperature of a gas is a measure of the:
o: Total potential energy of its molecules
Total number of molecules in the container
Average translational kinetic energy of its molecules
x: Absolute temperature is proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules. Heat flows from higher to lower temperature, i.e. from faster-moving molecules on average to slower ones.

q: Two bodies in contact are said to be in thermal equilibrium when they have the same:
x: Thermal equilibrium means there is no net flow of heat between the bodies, which happens when their temperatures are equal. Their internal energies and specific heats can still be very different.

q: 1 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 2 kg of water at 30 °C in an insulated container. Ignoring heat losses, the final temperature of the mixture is:
x: Heat lost = heat gained: 1 × c × (90 − T) = 2 × c × (T − 30), so 90 − T = 2T − 60 and T = 50 °C. 60 °C is the simple average, which ignores the unequal masses.

q: A hot steel spoon at 60 °C is pushed into a large block of ice at −5 °C. The block has far more internal energy than the spoon. Heat flows:
o: From the ice to the spoon, because the ice has more internal energy
From the spoon to the ice, because the spoon is at a higher temperature
In neither direction, because their internal energies balance
From the ice to the spoon, because the ice has a larger mass
x: The direction of heat flow is decided by temperature, not by the total internal energy or mass. The spoon is hotter, so heat flows from the spoon into the ice.

q: Body X (mass 1 kg, specific heat 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 100 °C is placed in contact with body Y (mass 1 kg, specific heat 800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 10 °C in an insulated box. The common final temperature is:
x: 400(100 − T) = 800(T − 10) gives 40 000 + 8000 = 1200T, so T = 40 °C. 70 °C comes from swapping the two specific heats; 55 °C is the plain average.

q: Body X is in thermal equilibrium with body Y, and body Y is in thermal equilibrium with body Z. Which statement is correct?
o: X and Z are at the same temperature
X and Z must have the same internal energy
Heat will flow from X to Z when they touch
x: X and Y have the same temperature and Y and Z have the same temperature, so X and Z are at the same temperature and no heat flows between them. Equal temperature does not mean equal internal energy.

q: The SI unit of specific heat is:
x: Specific heat is the heat per kilogram per kelvin, so its unit is J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the unit of molar specific heat, and J K⁻¹ is the unit of heat capacity.

q: In physics, heat is best described as:
o: Energy transferred from one body to another because of a temperature difference
The total kinetic energy of all the molecules of a body
A measure of how hot or cold a body is
The energy a body holds because of its mass
x: Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference. The total molecular energy of a body is its internal energy, and 'how hot a body is' describes temperature.

q: The main difference between specific heat and molar specific heat of a substance is that molar specific heat refers to:
o: One gram of the substance instead of one kilogram
One mole of the substance instead of one kilogram
A rise of 1 °C instead of 1 K
x: Specific heat is the heat needed per kilogram per kelvin; molar specific heat is the heat needed per mole per kelvin. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K, so that is not the difference.

q: A clinical thermometer placed under a patient's tongue for a minute shows the patient's body temperature because:
o: The thermometer reaches thermal equilibrium with the body
The thermometer stores the heat of the body permanently
Heat keeps flowing into the thermometer as long as it is in the mouth
The mercury has a higher temperature than the body
x: After a short time no net heat flows between the thermometer and the body, so both are at the same temperature and the reading equals body temperature.

q: A substance has specific heat c and molar mass M (in kg mol⁻¹). Its molar specific heat C is given by:
x: One mole has a mass of M kilograms, so the heat per mole per kelvin is M times the heat per kilogram per kelvin: C = Mc.

q: A gas expands at constant pressure P, and its volume increases by ΔV. The work done by the gas is:
x: Work done by the gas = force × distance = (PA) × Δy = PΔV, where AΔy is the change in volume.

q: The specific heat of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and its molar mass is 0.018 kg mol⁻¹. The molar specific heat of water is about:
x: C = Mc = 0.018 × 4200 = 75.6 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Dividing instead of multiplying gives about 2.3 × 10⁵.

q: A gas at a constant pressure of 2 × 10⁵ Pa expands from 1 × 10⁻³ m³ to 3 × 10⁻³ m³. The work done by the gas is:
x: W = PΔV = 2 × 10⁵ × (3 − 1) × 10⁻³ = 400 J. 600 J uses the final volume instead of the change in volume.

q: Helium has a molar specific heat at constant volume of 12.5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and a molar mass of 0.004 kg mol⁻¹. Its specific heat at constant volume is:
x: c = C/M = 12.5/0.004 = 3125 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. 0.05 comes from multiplying by the molar mass instead of dividing.

q: A gas is compressed at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 5 litres to 2 litres (1 litre = 10⁻³ m³). The work done on the gas is:
x: ΔV = 3 litres = 3 × 10⁻³ m³, so work done on the gas = PΔV = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 3 × 10⁻³ = 300 J. 3 × 10⁵ J forgets to convert litres to m³.

q: 2 mol of a gas with molar specific heat at constant volume 20 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is heated at constant volume through 10 K. The heat supplied is:
x: Q = nCvΔT = 2 × 20 × 10 = 400 J. 200 J forgets the number of moles.

q: On a pressure–volume graph of a gas changing from one state to another, the work done by the gas is given by the:
o: Area between the curve and the volume axis
Pressure at the final point multiplied by the final volume
x: Work done = ∫P dV, which is the area under the P–V curve down to the volume axis. For constant pressure this area is the rectangle PΔV.

q: Two different molar specific heats (at constant volume and at constant pressure) are defined for a gas but are not usually needed for a solid because:
o: A gas expands much more on heating, so the heat needed depends strongly on the conditions
A gas has no definite mass
A solid cannot be heated at constant pressure
The molar mass of a gas changes when it is heated
x: When a gas is heated at constant pressure it expands a lot and does work, so it needs more heat than at constant volume. Solids and liquids expand very little, so the two values are almost equal.

q: A gas is heated in a closed rigid steel cylinder, so its volume cannot change. The work done by the gas is:
o: Equal to the rise in pressure times the volume
x: Work done by a gas is PΔV. In a rigid container ΔV = 0, so no work is done even though the pressure rises.

q: The specific heat of copper is 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. If the mass of a copper sample is doubled, its specific heat becomes:
x: Specific heat is a property of the material, not of the sample size, so it stays 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. The heat needed for a given temperature rise doubles, but that is the heat capacity.

q: When a gas in a cylinder is compressed by pushing the piston in, the work done by the gas is:
o: Positive, because energy is given to the gas
Zero, because the gas does not move
Always equal to the heat lost by the gas
x: Work done by the gas is PΔV and ΔV is negative in a compression, so the work done by the gas is negative; equivalently, positive work is done on the gas by the piston.

q: Hydrogen (molar mass 2 g mol⁻¹) and oxygen (molar mass 32 g mol⁻¹) have the same molar specific heat at constant volume. The ratio of the specific heat of hydrogen to that of oxygen (per kilogram) is:
x: Specific heat c = C/M. With the same C, c is inversely proportional to molar mass: c(H₂)/c(O₂) = 32/2 = 16. One kilogram of hydrogen contains 16 times as many moles.

q: A gas in a cylinder at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa pushes a piston of area 0.02 m² outward through 0.1 m. The work done by the gas is:
x: ΔV = area × distance = 0.02 × 0.1 = 2 × 10⁻³ m³, so W = PΔV = 1.5 × 10⁵ × 2 × 10⁻³ = 300 J.

q: The heat capacity of a 0.5 kg block of aluminium (specific heat 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is:
x: Heat capacity = mc = 0.5 × 900 = 450 J K⁻¹. Unlike specific heat, heat capacity depends on the mass of the body.

q: The product of pressure and volume, PV, has the same SI unit as:
x: Pa × m³ = N m⁻² × m³ = N m = J, the unit of energy and work. That is why PΔV gives work in joules.

q: The specific heat of a substance is the heat required to raise the temperature of:
o: 1 mol of the substance by 1 K
1 kg of the substance from its melting point to its boiling point
1 kg of the substance by 1 K
x: Specific heat c is the heat needed per kilogram per kelvin, c = Q/(mΔT). For the whole body it is the heat capacity; for one mole it is the molar specific heat.

q: 2 mol of an ideal gas is heated at constant pressure so that its temperature rises by 50 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the work done by the gas is:
x: At constant pressure PΔV = nRΔT (from PV = nRT), so W = 2 × 8.3 × 50 = 830 J. 415 J forgets the 2 moles.

q: The rms speed of the molecules of a gas is 400 m s⁻¹ at 27 °C. If the gas is heated to 927 °C, the rms speed becomes:
x: v_rms ∝ √T with T in kelvin: T rises from 300 K to 1200 K, four times, so v_rms doubles to 800 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 1600 m s⁻¹; using the Celsius ratio 927/27 gives about 2340 m s⁻¹.

q: A gas of density 1.5 kg m⁻³ has an rms molecular speed of 400 m s⁻¹. From kinetic theory, its pressure is:
x: P = ⅓ρ⟨v²⟩ = ⅓ × 1.5 × (400)² = ⅓ × 1.5 × 1.6 × 10⁵ = 8 × 10⁴ Pa. Leaving out the ⅓ gives 2.4 × 10⁵ Pa; forgetting to square the speed gives 200 Pa.

q: 0.5 mol of an ideal gas is kept in a container of volume 8.31 litres at 127 °C. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and 1 litre = 10⁻³ m³, the pressure of the gas is:
x: P = nRT/V = 0.5 × 8.31 × 400 / (8.31 × 10⁻³) = 200/10⁻³ = 2 × 10⁵ Pa, with T = 127 + 273 = 400 K. Using 127 instead of 400 gives 6.35 × 10⁴ Pa; leaving the volume in litres gives 200 Pa.

q: If the absolute temperature of an ideal gas is doubled, the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules:
x: The average translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)kT, so it is directly proportional to the kelvin temperature: doubling T doubles it. The √2 factor applies to the rms speed, not the energy.

q: Taking the Boltzmann constant k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at 27 °C is:
x: KE = (3/2)kT = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 = 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J. Writing kT alone gives 4.14 × 10⁻²¹ J; using 27 instead of 300 K gives 5.59 × 10⁻²² J.

q: Hydrogen (molar mass 2 g mol⁻¹) and oxygen (molar mass 32 g mol⁻¹) are at the same temperature. The ratio of the rms speed of hydrogen molecules to that of oxygen molecules is:
x: v_rms = √(3RT/M), so at the same T, v_H/v_O = √(M_O/M_H) = √(32/2) = √16 = 4. Forgetting the square root gives 16; inverting the ratio gives 1/4.

q: An ideal gas is sealed in a rigid container, and its molecules have an rms speed of 500 m s⁻¹. The gas is heated until its pressure is doubled. The new rms speed is about:
x: At constant volume P ∝ T, so doubling the pressure doubles the kelvin temperature; v_rms ∝ √T, so the speed becomes 500 × √2 ≈ 707 m s⁻¹. Taking v_rms ∝ T gives 1000 m s⁻¹.

q: A gas at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa has a density of 1.2 kg m⁻³. The rms speed of its molecules is:
x: From P = ⅓ρv², v_rms = √(3P/ρ) = √(3 × 10⁵/1.2) = √(2.5 × 10⁵) = 500 m s⁻¹. Leaving out the 3 gives about 289 m s⁻¹; forgetting the square root gives 2.5 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

q: A 1.2 litre flask holds an ideal gas at a pressure of 1.38 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 27 °C. Taking k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and 1 litre = 10⁻³ m³, the number of gas molecules in the flask is:
x: N = PV/kT = (1.38 × 10⁵ × 1.2 × 10⁻³)/(1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300) = 165.6/(4.14 × 10⁻²¹) = 4.0 × 10²². Using 27 instead of 300 K gives about 4.4 × 10²³; leaving the volume in litres gives 4.0 × 10²⁵.

q: An ideal gas is compressed slowly to half its volume at constant temperature, and its pressure doubles. According to kinetic theory, the pressure rises because the molecules:
o: Move faster on average and hit the walls harder
Become larger and fill more of the container
Attract each other more strongly at shorter distances
Hit the walls more often while their average speed stays the same
x: At constant temperature the average molecular kinetic energy, and so the average speed, is unchanged. In half the volume the number of molecules per unit volume doubles, so wall collisions per second double and the pressure doubles. Faster molecules would need a higher temperature.

q: In each cycle a heat engine absorbs 1000 J from a hot reservoir and rejects 700 J to a cold reservoir. Its efficiency is:
x: Work output = 1000 − 700 = 300 J, so efficiency = 300/1000 = 30%. Dividing the rejected heat by the input gives 70%; dividing the work by the rejected heat gives 43%.

q: A Carnot engine works between a source at 327 °C and a sink at 27 °C. Its efficiency is:
x: In kelvin, T_h = 600 K and T_c = 300 K, so η = 1 − T_c/T_h = 1 − 300/600 = 50%. Using Celsius temperatures gives 1 − 27/327 ≈ 92%.

q: A Carnot engine of efficiency 40% absorbs 2000 J of heat from its source in each cycle. The heat it rejects to the sink in each cycle is:
x: Work per cycle W = 0.40 × 2000 = 800 J, so heat rejected = 2000 − 800 = 1200 J. Giving the work instead of the rejected heat leads to 800 J; dividing by the efficiency gives 5000 J.

q: A Carnot engine has its sink at 300 K and an efficiency of 25%. The temperature of its source is:
x: 1 − T_c/T_h = 0.25 gives T_c/T_h = 0.75, so T_h = 300/0.75 = 400 K. Check: 1 − 300/400 = 0.25. Multiplying 300 by 1.25 gives 375 K; dividing 300 by 0.25 gives 1200 K.

q: A Carnot engine with its sink at 27 °C has an efficiency of 40%. Keeping the sink temperature fixed, by how much must the source temperature be raised to make the efficiency 50%?
x: With T_c = 300 K: for 40%, T_h = 300/0.6 = 500 K; for 50%, T_h = 300/0.5 = 600 K, so the rise is 100 K. Wrongly taking efficiency as T_c/T_h gives 750 K and 600 K, a difference of 150 K.

q: A refrigerator keeps its freezer at −23 °C in a room at 27 °C. Its maximum possible (Carnot) coefficient of performance is:
x: COP = T_c/(T_h − T_c) = 250/(300 − 250) = 250/50 = 5, with temperatures in kelvin. Using T_h/(T_h − T_c) = 6 is the heat-pump figure; 300/250 = 1.2 uses the wrong formula.

q: In each cycle a refrigerator removes 600 J of heat from its cold compartment while 150 J of work is done on it by the compressor. The heat it gives out to the room in each cycle is:
x: By energy conservation, heat delivered to the room = heat removed + work done = 600 + 150 = 750 J. Subtracting the work instead of adding it gives 450 J.

q: According to the second law of thermodynamics, which of the following is impossible?
o: Turning a given amount of work completely into heat by friction
Heat flowing by itself from a hot body to a cold body
A refrigerator moving heat from a cold body to a hot body when work is done on it
An engine that, working in a cycle, takes heat from a single reservoir and turns all of it into work
x: The Kelvin statement says no engine working in a cycle can convert all the heat taken from a single reservoir into work; some must be rejected to a colder sink. Work can be turned fully into heat, and a refrigerator can move heat to a hotter body if work is supplied.

q: A Carnot engine works between 400 K and 300 K. Which single change gives it the greatest efficiency?
o: Lowering the sink temperature to 250 K
Raising the source temperature to 450 K
x: η = 1 − T_c/T_h: lowering the sink gives 1 − 250/400 = 37.5%; raising the source gives 1 − 300/450 ≈ 33%; raising both gives 1 − 350/450 ≈ 22%; lowering both gives 1 − 250/350 ≈ 29%. A change in the sink has the larger effect because T_c is the smaller temperature.

q: The efficiency of a Carnot engine depends only on:
o: The temperatures of its source and sink
The nature of the working substance
The amount of working substance used
The speed at which the engine runs
x: η = 1 − T_c/T_h for every reversible (Carnot) engine, whatever the working substance or its amount, so only the two reservoir temperatures matter.

q: The SI unit of entropy is:
x: Entropy change ΔS = ΔQ/T, heat in joules divided by temperature in kelvin, so its unit is J K⁻¹. J kg⁻¹ is the unit of latent heat.

q: A block of ice at 0 °C absorbs 2.73 × 10⁵ J of heat and melts at constant temperature. The entropy change of the ice is:
x: ΔS = ΔQ/T = 2.73 × 10⁵/273 = 1.0 × 10³ J K⁻¹, an increase. Multiplying by T instead of dividing gives 7.45 × 10⁷ J K⁻¹; dividing T by Q gives 10⁻³.

q: Steam at 100 °C condenses to water at 100 °C and gives out 7.46 × 10⁵ J of heat. The entropy change of the steam is:
x: Heat leaves the steam, so its entropy falls: ΔS = −7.46 × 10⁵/373 = −2.0 × 10³ J K⁻¹. Dividing by 100 instead of 373 K gives 7.46 × 10³; dropping the minus sign ignores that heat was lost.

q: 1200 J of heat flows by conduction from a large reservoir at 600 K to a large reservoir at 300 K, with both temperatures unchanged. The total entropy change of the two reservoirs is:
x: Hot reservoir: −1200/600 = −2 J K⁻¹; cold reservoir: +1200/300 = +4 J K⁻¹; total = +2 J K⁻¹, an increase, as expected for an irreversible process. Adding the magnitudes gives 6 J K⁻¹.

q: For a system and its surroundings taken together, the total entropy during a reversible process:
x: In a reversible process the entropy gained by one part equals the entropy lost by the other, so the total is unchanged. It increases only in irreversible (real) processes and never decreases.

q: The working substance of a Carnot engine goes through one complete cycle. Its change in entropy over the cycle is:
o: Equal to the work done divided by the sink temperature
x: Entropy is a state function, and after a complete cycle the substance is back in its starting state, so its entropy change is zero.

q: An ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly at 27 °C and absorbs 600 J of heat. The entropy change of the gas is:
x: ΔS = Q/T = 600/300 = +2 J K⁻¹ with T = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Using 27 instead of 300 gives 22.2 J K⁻¹; inverting the ratio gives 0.5 J K⁻¹.

q: A gas expands reversibly and adiabatically. During this expansion the entropy of the gas:
x: In an adiabatic process no heat enters or leaves (ΔQ = 0), and for a reversible process ΔS = ΔQ/T = 0, so the entropy stays constant (an isentropic process). The temperature falls, but entropy does not change.

q: A reversible engine takes 1000 J of heat from a source at 500 K and rejects heat to a sink at 300 K. Using the fact that the total entropy change of the two reservoirs is zero, the heat rejected per cycle is:
x: Entropy lost by the source = 1000/500 = 2 J K⁻¹ = entropy gained by the sink, so Q_c = 2 × 300 = 600 J (and work = 400 J, efficiency 40%). Giving the work gives 400 J; using 1000 × 500/300 gives 1667 J.

q: In which of these processes does the entropy of the substance decrease?
o: A gas expanding freely into a vacuum
x: Freezing removes heat and puts molecules into an ordered crystal, so the entropy of the water falls. Melting, evaporation and free expansion all increase disorder and entropy.
